chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Said from Safwan from Ibn Muskhan from al-Mu'alla ibn Khunays said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'What is sufficient regarding witnesses for Mut'ah (temporary marriage)?' He said: 'One man and two women who witness it.' I said: 'What if they cannot find anyone?' He said: 'They will not be lacking [in validity].' I said: 'What if they fear that someone will learn of it? Is one man sufficient for them?' He said: 'Yes.'

I said: 'May I be your ransom, were the Muslims during the time of the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) marrying without a clear proof/witness?' He said: 'No, and it does not contradict the first report, because the report does not prohibit the validity of Mut'ah marriage without a witness; rather, it implies that during the time of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), they did not marry except with a witness, and that is the preferable option.'

And just because that was not practiced in that era does not indicate that it is forbidden, just as we know that here there are many permissible things and others that were not used in that time, and that does not indicate their prohibition.
And the report came in the place of precaution rather than obligation, so that the woman would not consider that to be indecency if she were not from those of knowledge.
And that which reveals what we mentioned.
ai.seo_question: What are the witness requirements for Shia temporary marriage (Mut'ah)?
ai.summary: In this hadith from al-istibsar, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that while one man and two women are the standard witnesses for Mut'ah, a single male witness suffices if necessary, and the Prophet’s practice of requiring witnesses was a matter of precaution (ihtiyat) rather than a strict condition for validity. This distinction highlights the Shia jurisprudential view that the absence of witnesses does not invalidate the contract, distinguishing it from permanent marriage where witnesses are often considered a pillar. The Imam further explains that practices not common in the Prophet's era do not imply prohibition, reinforcing the flexibility of temporary marriage contracts.
